extra.message: User input from request.GET['expr'] is passed directly to eval(), allowing arbitrary Python code execution. Although __builtins__ is set to {}, this can be bypassed using Python object introspection (e.g.,().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()) to achieve remote code execution.

User-controlled data from request.body or request.GET['blob'] is deserialized using pickle.loads(), which can execute arbitrary code. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve remote code execution on the server.

User input from request.GET['fragment'] is concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered. Jinja2 templates can execute arbitrary code through expressions like {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('cmd').read()}}, enabling remote code execution. The response is served as text/html.

User-controlled JSON from request.body is passed directly as a MongoDB query filter via find_one(query). If the 'filter' key is absent, the entire payload is used as the query. This allows NoSQL injection operators like {'$gt': ''} or {'$where': 'sleep(5000)'} to bypass filters or extract data.

extra.message: User input from request.GET['name'] is used directly in a file path (BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name) without sanitization, and request.body is written to that path. An attacker can use path traversal sequences like '../../../etc/cron.d/malicious' to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

The random module (which uses a Mersenne Twister PRNG, not cryptographically secure) is used to generate security-relevant tokens/codes. An attacker who observes some outputs can predict future values. The secrets module should be used instead.

extra.message: Social Security Numbers (SSN) and credit card numbers are written to a JSON file in plaintext. Additionally, these sensitive values are passed via GET parameters which are typically logged in web server access logs and browser history.
Environment variables (DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE) and filesystem paths (BASE_EXPORT_DIR) are returned in the JSON response, exposing server configuration details that could aid an attacker.

The 'state' field of a ledger object is set from user-controlled input (payload['state'] or request.GET['state']), allowing an attacker to set the approval state to any value regardless of the actual balance, bypassing business logic authorization checks.

Authorization is determined by the value of a user-controlled cookie ('ops_badge') or header ('x-ops-badge'), which can be trivially set to 'lead' by an attacker to gain elevated access with 'full' payroll and 'open' casework permissions.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: Hardcoded verifier values ('north': '4812', 'south': '5930') are used as shared secrets for authentication. These cannot be rotated without code changes and are visible to anyone with source code access.

A cookie is set using set_cookie() without specifying HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags. This makes the cookie accessible to JavaScript (XSS risk), sent over HTTP (interception risk), and vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.

cwe: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute

extra.message: The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value 'django-insecure-local-dev-only-change-in-production'. If the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set in production, this known key is used, allowing session forgery, CSRF token bypass, and data signing attacks.
The database password has a hardcoded fallback value 'hrpayroll123'. If the DB_PASSWORD environment variable is not set in production, this known password is used to connect to the database.

DEBUG defaults to 'True' when the DEBUG environment variable is not set. In production, this would expose detailed error pages with stack traces, settings values, and SQL queries, significantly aiding attackers.

The api_employees endpoint is marked @csrf_exempt and uses session-based authentication as a fallback (via _api_auth). When a browser-based session is used instead of an API key, CSRF protection is disabled, allowing cross-site request forgery attacks.

The comp_request_submit view performs a state-changing operation (changing status to SUBMITTED) without checking request.method. A simple GET request to this URL will execute the change. Since Django's CSRF middleware only protects POST requests, this is vulnerable to CSRF via GET (e.g., through a link in an email or malicious website).
The comp_request_manager_approve view performs a state-changing operation (manager approval) without checking request.method. A GET request will execute the approval, bypassing CSRF protection.
The comp_request_hr_approve view performs a state-changing operation (HR approval) without checking request.method. A GET request will execute the approval, bypassing CSRF protection.
The task_start view changes task status to IN_PROGRESS without checking request.method. A GET request will execute the state change, bypassing CSRF protection.
The task_approve view changes task status to APPROVED without checking request.method. A GET request will execute the approval, bypassing CSRF protection.
The task_reject view changes task status to REJECTED without checking request.method. A GET request will execute the rejection, bypassing CSRF protection.
The task_waive view changes task status to WAIVED without checking request.method. A GET request will execute the state change, bypassing CSRF protection.

The policy_detail view does not check the policy's audience field. While policy_list filters by audience, any authenticated user can access any policy (including HR-only or Manager-only policies) by directly visiting the URL with the policy's primary key.

Webhook deletion (WebhookEndpoint.objects.filter(pk=wh_id).delete()) does not filter by the requesting user, allowing any HR admin to delete webhooks created by other users. There is no ownership check on the webhook being deleted.

When importing employees via CSV, a default password 'changeme123' is used if no password is provided in the CSV row. This creates accounts with a known, weak password that may never be changed, allowing unauthorized access.
